introduction-the-zombie-infrastructure-p.core: Organisations add tools and services but rarely remove them. Zombie infrastructure (old versions, unused services, legacy platforms) costs money, multiplies the security surface and support load, so deprecation is an engineering discipline.

first_principles.problem: Five deploy systems, three logging stacks and dozens of unused services all need patching and support.
derivation: **Inventory** what exists and who uses it.

analogy.title: A garage that's never cleared out
analogy.story: Eventually you can't park the car because of everything you're keeping just in case.
analogy.breaks: Some legacy systems are critical, so understand the usage before removing anything.

example.title: Tool sprawl audit
flow: Plan: consolidate to 1 CI, 1 logging, delete the zero-traffic services

check.q: Why is zombie infrastructure costly even if unused?
check.a: It still needs patching, support and money, and it expands the security surface.

the-scream-test-the-nuclear-option.core: A scream test turns something off to see who complains, revealing hidden users when there's no other data. It's effective but risky, so use it only after usage analysis, with notice, a quick restore plan and outside critical periods.

first_principles.problem: Nobody knows whether an old service is used, and logs and owners are missing.
truths: Users reveal themselves when something breaks.
derivation: First **check the usage data** (logs, metrics, network flows).
**Turn it off** (but don't delete) in a low-risk window.
**Restore fast** if anyone screams, and record the users.

analogy.title: Unplugging cables to find what they power
analogy.story: Pull a plug from the mystery power strip and see which device goes dark, but have a hand ready to plug it back in.
analogy.breaks: In critical systems a scream may come from a major outage, so avoid it there.

example.title: A safe scream test
flow: Logs show 2 requests/day from unknown IP
A batch team screams → restore, plan migration

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The hidden dependency is found safely.

check.q: Why should a scream test turn things off rather than delete them?
check.a: So the service can be restored immediately if an unknown user depends on it.

brownouts-the-safer-alternative.core: A brownout makes a deprecated service temporarily and partially unavailable (scheduled short outages, a percentage of requests failing with clear deprecation errors) to get consumers' attention gradually before the final shutdown.

first_principles.problem: Deprecation emails are ignored until the day the service is switched off, and then there's panic.
truths: People ignore warnings that have no consequences.
derivation: Run **short brownouts** (e.g. 10 minutes) with error messages pointing to migration docs.
**Track** who hits the brownouts and contact them.

analogy.title: Dimming the lights before closing
analogy.story: A shop dims the lights and announces closing so customers finish up, rather than plunging into darkness.
analogy.breaks: Brownouts still cause brief failures, so avoid them for critical paths without consent.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Most consumers migrate before the shutdown.

check.a: A scheduled, temporary partial outage of a deprecated service that alerts consumers to migrate before the final shutdown.

automated-migration-the-codemod-strategy.core: Developers resist deprecation mostly because of migration effort. Codemods (automated code transformations) and migration bots let the platform team open the PRs that move teams to the new API or tool, turning 'please migrate' into 'please review'.

first_principles.problem: Teams agree the new library is better but never find time to migrate 200 call sites.
derivation: **Run them across repos** and open PRs (bots, batch changes).
**Track** merge progress; handle the remaining manual cases.

analogy.title: A moving company that packs for you
analogy.story: People delay moving because packing is hard; a service that packs makes moving easy.
analogy.breaks: Codemods can't handle every edge case, so budget for manual follow-ups.

example.title: Migrating a logging API
flow: CI passes on 165; 15 need manual work

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Deprecation finished in weeks, not years.

check.q: Why are codemods effective for deprecations?
check.a: They remove the main barrier, migration effort, by automating changes so teams only need to review PRs.

managing-psychological-resistance.core: Engineers resist deprecation because of familiarity, sunk-cost feelings, fear of breaking things and competing priorities. Address it with empathy, clear 'why', good timelines, migration support, early adopters and recognition, plus firm deadlines.

first_principles.problem: Teams cling to the old tool and escalate complaints, and the deprecation stalls for years.
derivation: **Celebrate** migrators; hold **firm deadlines**, with exceptions only through a defined process.

analogy.title: Switching to a new car after 10 years
analogy.story: You know every button in the old one; the new one feels awkward until someone shows you around.
analogy.breaks: Some resistance points to real gaps in the replacement, so fix them.

check.q: Name two common psychological reasons engineers resist deprecations.
check.a: For example, familiarity with the old tool and fear of breaking things (also sunk cost and competing priorities).
